titel: The Path to a Democratic Supermajority

einzeiler: How Democrats can build a lasting supermajority through a broad, heterodox big tent.
kurzfassung: Adam Jentleson discusses how Democrats can move past narrow majorities to build an enduring supermajority. He argues for a big-tent approach that embraces ideological diversity, economic populism, and local authenticity. The conversation also explores Senate rules, filibuster reform, and party leadership for the upcoming congressional term.
stichpunkte: Supermajority thinking aims to represent more than the bare minimum of voters to secure long-term power.
Democrats made historic gains in unlikely regions by running candidates who reflect local values.
The party must embrace heterodoxy and avoid rigid ideological purity tests.
Economic populism and affordability serve as unifying themes across different party factions.
Eliminating the filibuster would allow for more legislative flexibility and dissenting votes within the caucus.
Party leaders should focus on broad areas of agreement like expanding universal healthcare.
Senate leadership should act as a bridge to the next generation of politicians.

clips.hook: Building a real mandate instead of just aiming for fifty plus one
clips.text: The guest explains that political strategy should focus on assembling broad coalitions to hold power over a decade rather than just scraping by with minimal margins.

clips.hook: Normalizing disagreement and voting against party leadership
clips.text: An examination of historical political norms where politicians could regularly dissent from their party without facing severe consequences.

beschreibung:
Democrats are on track to have more power in the next Congress than they’ve had since 2009. How can they navigate the divides in a party that now stretches from Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan to Adam Hamilton in Kansas? How do they prevent all their new voters in this election from flipping back in the next one? Can they turn this victory into a springboard to an even bigger and more durable Democratic majority in 2028 and beyond?
We will have two episodes that try to answer these questions from different angles, one from the center of the party and one from the left. First, representing the more center view, we have Adam Jentleson, the founder and president of the Searchlight Institute, a Washington think tank. Jentleson is a veteran of the Senate; he served as deputy chief of staff to the former Senate majority leader Harry Reid and chief of staff to Senator John Fetterman. He’s also the author of two books, “Kill Switch: The Rise of the Modern Senate and the Crippling of American Democracy,” and “Supermajority: How Democrats Can Build Lasting Power,” which came out in September.
Note: An earlier version of this episode misstated the religious denomination of Adam Hamilton. He is a United Methodist minister, not an Episcopal minister.
